title: Stage A2.2 — Future, Conditional, & Object Pronouns
description: Talk about future plans, make predictions and requests, express what you would do in hypothetical situations, and use object pronouns to avoid repetition. This stage builds on the preterite and imperfect from A1.2 and A2.1 by introducing forward-looking and hypothetical language.

grammar.title: Simple Future (Futuro Simple) — Regular Conjugation
grammar.content:
The future tense expresses actions that will happen, predictions, and promises. Unlike English, Spanish future tense keeps the FULL infinitive as the stem and adds the endings directly — so -AR, -ER, and -IR verbs share the same set of endings. This makes it one of the easiest tenses to learn in Spanish.

Future endings (add to the full infinitive):
- yo: -é
- tú: -ás
- él/ella/usted: -á
- nosotros: -emos
- vosotros: -éis
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -án

Examples:
- hablar → hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán
- comer → comeré, comerás, comerá, comeremos, comeréis, comerán
- vivir → viviré, vivirás, vivirá, viviremos, viviréis, vivirán
examples: El año que viene viajaré a España. (Next year I will travel to Spain.)
Mañana compraré pan en la panadería. (Tomorrow I will buy bread at the bakery.)
Creo que lloverá mañana. (I think it will rain tomorrow.)
¿Vivirás aquí mucho tiempo? (Will you live here for a long time?)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian future is built with 'voi/vi/va/vom/veti/va' + infinitive: 'voi vorbi' (I will speak). Spanish is actually simpler — you just add one set of endings to the infinitive, no separate helper verb needed. The Spanish future is one word where Romanian needs two.

grammar.title: Future — Irregular Stems (TENDR-, DIR-, POND-, SAGR-, SALD-, PODR-, QUERR-, DIR-)
grammar.content:
Some of the most common Spanish verbs have irregular stems in the future tense, but they STILL use the same regular endings. The key ones to memorize:

- CABER → cabré (to fit)
- DECIR → dir- (to say/tell) → diré, dirás, dirá, diremos, diréis, dirán
- HABER → habré (to have — auxiliary) → habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán
- HACER → haré (to do/make) → haré, harás, hará, haremos, haréis, harán
- METER → metré (not commonly tested)
- PODER → podré (to be able to) → podré, podrás, podrá, podremos, podréis, podrán
- PONER → pondré (to put) → pondré, pondrás, pondrá, pondremos, pondréis, pondrán
- QUERER → querré (to want) → querré, querrás, querrá, querremos, querréis, querrán
- SALIR → saldré (to leave) → saldré, saldrás, saldrá, saldremos, saldréis, saldrán
- SABER → sabré (to know) → sabré, sabrás, sabrá, sabremos, sabréis, sabrán
- TENER → tendré (to have) → tendré, tendrás, tendrá, tendremos, tendréis, tendrán
- VENIR → vendré (to come) → vendré, vendrás, vendrá, vendremos, vendréis, vendrán

Mnemonic: 'Had My Dad Put Six Small Pear Trees In The Garden' — HABER, HACER, DECIR, PONER, SALIR, PODER, QUERER, SABER, TENER, VENIR.
examples: Tendré una reunión importante mañana. (I will have an important meeting tomorrow.)
No podré asistir a la fiesta. (I won't be able to attend the party.)
¿Qué me dirás? (What will you tell me?)
Ella vendrá con nosotros. (She will come with us.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian irregular future stems work similarly — they change the stem before adding the future marker. Spanish irregulars are limited to about 12 common verbs, and they all drop the final vowel of the infinitive before adding -r. This pattern is consistent across all persons.

grammar.title: Conditional (Condicional Simple) — Regular Conjugation
grammar.content:
The conditional expresses what 'would' happen — it's used for polite requests, hypothetical situations, and reported speech. The conditional is remarkably easy: take the FULL infinitive as the stem and add these endings:

Conditional endings (add to the full infinitive):
- yo: -ía
- tú: -ías
- él/ella/usted: -ía
- nosotros: -íamos
- vosotros: -íais
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -ían

Examples:
- hablar → hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablaríais, hablarían
- comer → comería, comerías, comería, comeríamos, comeríais, comerían
- vivir → viviría, vivirías, viviría, viviríamos, viviríais, vivirían

Notice: the conditional endings (-ía, -ías, -ía...) are EXACTLY the same as the imperfect -ER/-IR endings. This is a common source of confusion — context tells you which tense is being used.
examples: Me gustaría visitar México un día. (I would like to visit Mexico one day.)
¿Podrías ayudarme con esto? (Could you help me with this?)
Si tuviera dinero, compraría una casa. (If I had money, I would buy a house.)
Ella me dijo que vendría. (She told me she would come.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian conditional also uses the particle 'aș/ai/ar/ăm/ăți/ar' + infinitive: 'aș vorbi' (I would speak). Spanish is structurally different — it fuses everything into one word. The Spanish -ía endings are similar in sound to Romanian's 'aș' but more flexible since they vary by person. Both languages use the conditional for polite requests: 'Could you...?'.

grammar.title: Conditional — Irregular Stems (Same as Future)
grammar.content:
The conditional shares the same irregular stems as the future tense, but uses the conditional endings (-ía, -ías, etc.) instead. This means the stem changes are memorized once and applied to both tenses:

- tener → tendría (I would have)
- poner → pondría (I would put)
- salir → saldría (I would leave)
- poder → podría (I would be able to)
- querer → querría (I would want)
- decir → diría (I would say)
- hacer → haría (I would do/make)
- saber → sabría (I would know)
- venir → vendría (I would come)
- caber → cabría (I would fit)

These are the most commonly used conditional irregulars. The conditional irregulars are less frequently used than the future irregulars, but they appear often in polite conversation and hypothetical statements.
examples: ¿Podría pedirle un favor? (Could I ask you a favor?)
Ella diría la verdad. (She would tell the truth.)
Si pudiera, viajaría a Japón. (If I could, I would travel to Japan.)
No sabría responder esa pregunta. (I wouldn't know how to answer that question.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian conditional also uses the same irregular stem change: 'aș avea' (I would have) uses 'avea' as the stem. Spanish 'tendría' uses 'tendr-' as the stem. Both languages share the pattern of modifying the infinitive before adding the conditional marker. The Romanian 'aș' + infinitive is two words where Spanish uses one.

grammar.title: Past Perfect (Pretérito Pluscuamperfecto) — Haber + Past Participle
grammar.content:
The past perfect describes an action that happened BEFORE another past action. It's the 'past of the past.' You form it using the IMPERFECT of HABER + a past participle.

Imperfect of HABER:
- yo: había
- tú: habías
- él/ella/usted: había
- nosotros: habíamos
- vosotros: habíais
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: habían

Past participles:
- -AR → -ado (hablado)
- -ER → -ido (comido)
- -IR → -ido (vivido)
- Irregulars: hacer→hecho, decir→dicho, escribir→escrito, ver→visto, abrir→abierto, romper→roto, volver→vuelto, cubrir→cubierto

Usage: The past perfect is used when one past action clearly happened before another. In English, this is 'had + past participle.'

'Mientras yo estudiaba, mi hermano había terminado la tarea.' (While I was studying, my brother had finished the homework.)
examples: Ya había comido cuando llegaste. (I had already eaten when you arrived.)
Nunca había visto algo tan bonito. (I had never seen anything so beautiful.)
Cuando llegué al cine, la película ya había empezado. (When I arrived at the cinema, the movie had already started.)
Ellos se habían ido antes de que yo llegara. (They had left before I arrived.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian uses a similar structure: 'avusese' (had) + past participle. The Romanian past perfect (mai mult ca perfectul) is more complex with its own set of endings, but the concept is identical: one action happened before another past action. The Spanish 'había + participle' is much simpler to conjugate.

grammar.title: Object Pronoun Combinations (DO + IO in One Word)
grammar.content:
When you want to replace BOTH a direct and indirect object with pronouns, they combine into a SINGLE word. The indirect object pronoun (le/les) ALWAYS comes first, followed by the direct object pronoun (lo/la/los/las).

When le or les is followed by lo, la, los, or las, they change to SE + DO pronoun. This is one of the most important rules in Spanish pronoun usage.

Combinations:
- me + lo = melo (give it to me)
- me + la = mela
- te + lo = telo
- te + la = tela
- le + lo → se lo (give it to him/her)
- le + la → se la
- les + lo → se lo (give it to them)
- les + la → se la
- nos + lo = noslo (rare)
- os + lo = oslo (Spain only)

Placement rules:
- BEFORE conjugated verb: 'Te lo doy.' (I give it to you.)
- ATTACHED to infinitive: 'Voy a dártelo.' (I'm going to give it to you.)
- ATTACHED to gerund: 'Estoy preparándolo.' (I'm preparing it.)

When attached to an infinitive or gerund, add an accent mark to maintain proper stress.
examples: ¿Me lo puedes prestar? (Can you lend it to me?)
Se la recomendé al médico. (I recommended it to the doctor.)
Te lo voy a decir ahora mismo. (I'm going to tell it to you right now.)
Nos los compró en el mercado. (He bought them for us at the market.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian combines object pronouns similarly: 'mi-l' (it to me), 'ți-l' (it to you), 'i-l' (it to him/her). Spanish 'se lo' is equivalent to Romanian 'i-l'. The Romanian system is actually more similar to English word-for-word than Spanish, but the concept of combining pronouns is shared.

grammar.title: Verbs + Prepositions (Verbos + Preposiciones)
grammar.content:
Many Spanish verbs require a specific preposition before the next verb or noun. Unlike English, where prepositions are often intuitive, Spanish verbs lock onto their prepositions rigidly. Here are the most important A2.2 verb+preposition combinations:

- pensar EN (to think about)
  'Pienso en mi futuro.' (I'm thinking about my future.)

- salir CON (to go out with / to date)
  'Ella sale con su novio.' (She goes out with her boyfriend.)

- acostarse CON (to sleep with)
  'Se acuesta con sus padres.' (She goes to bed with her parents.)

- empezar A (to start to)
  'Empieza a llover.' (It starts to rain.)

- seguir CON (to continue with)
  'Sigo con mi trabajo.' (I continue with my work.)

- llamar A (to call)
  'Llamo a mi madre.' (I call my mother.)

- soñar CON/EN (to dream about)
  'Sueño con viajar a Japón.' (I dream of traveling to Japan.)

- depender DE (to depend on)
  'Depende de ti.' (It depends on you.)

- gustar A (to be pleasing to)
  'Le gusta a ella.' (She likes it.)
examples: ¿Con quién piensas ir al cine? (Who are you thinking of going to the cinema with?)
Siempre pienso en mis vacaciones. (I'm always thinking about my vacation.)
Ella sale con un chico de la clase. (She's going out with a guy from class.)
¿Con quién sueñas? (Who do you dream about?)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian also uses verb+preposition combinations, but the pairings are often different. For example, Romanian 'a gândi LA' (think at) vs Spanish 'pensar EN'. There's no reliable cross-language mapping — each verb+preposition pair must be memorized individually. However, Romanian speakers should note that Spanish prepositions (en, con, a, de) are the same words used in Romanian, which helps with recognition.

pronunciation.title: Stress in Future and Conditional Endings
pronunciation.content:
Future tense endings all carry the stress on the ending itself:

- yo: -é (always accented)
- tú: -ás (always accented)
- él/ella/usted: -á (always accented)
- nosotros: -emos (no accent — stress on the first syllable: ha-BLA-re-MOS)
- vosotros: -éis (always accented)
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -án (always accented)

Conditional endings all carry the stress on the -í:

- yo: -ía (stress on the í: ha-blar-ÍA)
- tú: -ías (ha-blar-ÍAS)
- él/ella/usted: -ía (ha-blar-ÍA)
- nosotros: -íamos (ha-blar-Ía-MOS — stress on the first syllable of the ending)
- vosotros: -íais (ha-blar-Ía-IS)
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -ían (ha-blar-ÍAN)

Important: The conditional endings are written with accents because they contain a stressed 'í'. This is the visual difference between the imperfect -ER/-IR and the conditional - both share the same sounds but the conditional always has the accent on the 'i'.
pronunciation.aid_note: Romanian future and conditional both place stress on the ending particle: 'voi vorbi' (stress on voi), 'aș vorbi' (stress on aș). Spanish conjugations naturally place stress on the ending too, so the rhythmic feel is similar. The key difference: Romanian uses separate words, Spanish fuses everything into one.

pronunciation.title: The Vowel Sound in Future and Conditional Endings
pronunciation.content:
The future and conditional endings contain only two vowel sounds, both of which are pure:

Future endings use 'a' and 'e': -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. These are all clean Spanish vowels — no diphthongs, no shifting sounds.

Conditional endings use 'i' and 'a': -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. The 'í' is always stressed and always sounds like 'ee'. The 'a' in -ía is a separate vowel sound, not a glide.

Critical distinction: Spanish 'comería' is pronounced 'ko-me-RI-a' (four distinct syllables, each vowel separate), NOT 'ko-MEER-yah' as English speakers might assume. The 'i' and 'a' in -ía are two separate syllables.

Also: the nosotros forms (hablaremos, hablaríamos) have NO accent mark because the stress falls naturally on the second-to-last syllable, which is the default rule.
pronunciation.aid_note: Romanian vowel pronunciation is very similar to Spanish — pure vowels without diphthongs. The main challenge for Romanian speakers is the Spanish conditional -ía which has four syllables (ha-blar-Í-a). In Romanian, 'aș vorbi' is naturally two syllables. Practice Spanish -ía by stretching it: 'ri-aaa' — two separate sounds, not one glide.

exercises.question: What is the future form of 'hablar' for 'yo'?
exercises.explanation: 'Hablaré' is the yo form of hablar in the future tense. The ending -é marks first-person singular future.

exercises.question: Which ending is the future 'tú' form?
exercises.explanation: '-ás' is the tú ending in the future tense: hablarás, comerás, vivirás.

exercises.question: Complete: 'El año que viene yo ____ (viajar) a México.' (Next year I will travel to Mexico.)
exercises.explanation: 'Viajaré' — add -é (yo future ending) to the infinitive viajar.

exercises.question: What is the future of 'tener' for 'él/ella/usted'?
exercises.explanation: 'Tendrá' — tener has the irregular stem tendr- in the future: tendr + á = tendrá.

exercises.question: What does the conditional express?
options: What would happen in hypothetical situations
exercises.explanation: The conditional expresses what 'would' happen — used for polite requests, hypothetical situations, and reported speech.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Me ____ (gustar) visitar Japón algún día.' (I would like to visit Japan one day.)
exercises.explanation: 'Gustaría' — conditional form. The conditional of -AR verbs uses -ía endings: gustaría, te gustaría, nos gustaría.

exercises.question: What is the conditional of 'poder' for 'yo'?
exercises.explanation: 'Podría' — poder has the irregular stem podr- in the conditional: podr + ía = podría.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Si tuviera dinero, yo ____ (comprar) una casa.' (If I had money, I would buy a house.)
exercises.explanation: 'Compraría' — conditional of comprar. This is a hypothetical 'si' clause: if I had... I would buy.

exercises.question: Which sentence uses the future tense correctly?
exercises.explanation: 'Mañana iré al cine' correctly uses the future tense with a future time marker (mañana = tomorrow).

exercises.question: What is the conditional of 'salir' for 'nosotros'?
exercises.explanation: 'Saldríamos' — salir uses the irregular stem saldr- + conditional ending -íamos = saldríamos.

exercises.question: Complete: '¿____ (podrías) abrir la ventana?' (Could you open the window?)
exercises.explanation: 'Podrías' — conditional of poder for tú. This is a polite request: could you...?

exercises.question: The past perfect is formed with:
exercises.explanation: The past perfect uses the IMPERFECT of haber (había, habías, había...) + past participle (hablado, comido, vivido). It describes an action that happened before another past action.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Cuando llegué, ya ____ (comer).' (When I arrived, they had already eaten.)
exercises.explanation: 'Habían comido' — past perfect: había/habías/había/habíamos/habíais/habían + past participle.

exercises.question: What is the past participle of 'hacer'?
exercises.explanation: 'Hecho' is the irregular past participle of hacer. Used in past perfect: había hecho (I had done).

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ella ya ____ (salir) cuando yo llamé.' (She had already left when I called.)
exercises.explanation: 'Había salido' — past perfect of salir: había + past participle salido.

exercises.question: What does 'se lo' replace in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: 'Se lo' replaces 'le/les + lo/la/los/las'. When le/les comes before lo/la/los/las, it changes to 'se' for pronunciation: 'Se lo di' = 'Le di lo.' (I gave it to him/her.)

exercises.question: Complete: 'Yo ____ (dar) el libro a María. → Yo ____ lo doy.' (I give the book to María → I give it to her.)
exercises.explanation: 'Se lo doy' — 'le' changes to 'se' when followed by 'lo': le + lo = se lo. 'Se lo doy' = I give it to him/her.

exercises.question: Where do object pronouns go with a conjugated verb?
options: At the end of the sentence
They don't go with conjugated verbs
exercises.explanation: Object pronouns go BEFORE the conjugated verb: 'Te lo doy' (I give it to you), not 'Doy te lo'.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Voy a ____ (decir) la verdad a ti. → Voy a ____ decir.' (I'm going to tell it to you.)
exercises.explanation: 'Decírtelo' — pronouns attach to the infinitive: te + lo + decir → decírtelo. An accent is added to maintain the stress on the í.

exercises.question: What preposition follows 'pensar' when meaning 'to think about'?
exercises.explanation: 'Pensar en' means 'to think about.' 'Pienso en ti' = I think about you. 'Pensar de' means 'to have an opinion about.'

exercises.question: What does 'salir con' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Salir con' means 'to go out with' or 'to date.' 'Ella sale con un chico' = She is dating a guy.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Siempre pienso ____ mis vacaciones.' (I always think about my vacation.)
exercises.explanation: 'Pienso en' — pensar requires the preposition 'en' when meaning 'to think about.' 'Pienso en ti' = I think about you.

exercises.question: Match each Spanish future form with its English meaning:
exercises.explanation: Future tense adds endings directly to the full infinitive. Note: nosotros uses -emos, which looks like the present nosotros form but the context tells you it's future.

exercises.question: Match each object pronoun combination with its English meaning:
exercises.explanation: Pronoun combinations: IO comes first, then DO. When le/les is before lo/la/los/las, it changes to 'se'.

exercises.question: Match each verb+preposition combination with its English meaning:
exercises.explanation: These verb+preposition combinations are fixed — you must memorize them as pairs. 'Acabar de + infinitive' means 'to have just done something': Acabo de llegar = I just arrived.

exercises.question: Complete the future tense conjugation table for the regular verb VIVIR:
exercises.explanation: Future tense adds endings directly to the full infinitive: viviré, vivirás, vivirá, viviremos, viviréis, vivirán.

exercises.question: Complete the conditional tense conjugation table for the regular verb ESTUDIAR:
exercises.explanation: Conditional tense adds endings directly to the full infinitive: estudiaría, estudiarías, estudiaría, estudiaríamos, estudiaríais, estudiarían.

exercises.question: Complete the future tense conjugation table for the irregular verb TENER:
exercises.explanation: TENER uses the irregular stem tendr- in the future: tendré, tendrás, tendrá, tendremos, tendréis, tendrán.

exercises.question: Complete the conditional tense conjugation table for the irregular verb PODER:
exercises.explanation: PODER uses the irregular stem podr- in the conditional: podría, podrías, podría, podríamos, podríais, podrían.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Mañana ____ (hacer) la compra en el supermercado.' (Tomorrow I will do the shopping at the supermarket.)
exercises.explanation: 'Haré' — hacer has the irregular stem har- in the future. 'Haré' (yo form) + 'la compra' = I will do the shopping.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Si yo ____ (poder), te ____ (ayudar).' (If I could, I would help you.)
exercises.explanation: 'Pudiera podría' — conditional sentence: imperfect subjunctive (si pudiera) + conditional (podría). This is a hypothetical: if I could, I would help.

exercises.question: Complete: '¿Me ____ (puedes) ____ (lo) ____ (decir)?' (Can you tell it to me?)
exercises.explanation: '¿Me lo puedes decir?' — pronouns go before the conjugated verb: me lo + puedes decir. Or with infinitive: ¿Puedes decírmelo? Both are correct.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ellos ya ____ (salir) cuando nosotros ____ (llegar).' (They had already left when we arrived.)
exercises.explanation: 'Habían salido' = past perfect (they had left). 'Llegamos' = preterite (we arrived). The past perfect action (salir) happened BEFORE the preterite action (llegar).

exercises.question: Complete: '¿Con quién ____ (piensas) ____ (ir) al cine?' (Who are you thinking of going to the cinema with?)
exercises.explanation: 'Piensas ir' — pensar requires 'en' for 'think about,' but here 'con quién' is the object. '¿Con quién piensas ir?' = Who are you thinking of going with?

exercises.question: What is the conditional of 'decir' for 'vosotros'?
exercises.explanation: 'Diríais' — decir uses the irregular stem dir- in the conditional: dir- + íais = diríais.

exercises.question: Which verb requires the preposition 'de' after it?
exercises.explanation: 'Dependen de' = to depend on. 'Depende de ti' = It depends on you. Pensar takes 'en,' salir takes 'con,' soñar takes 'con.'

exercises.question: Complete: 'No ____ (sé) la respuesta. — ____ (Sabrías) responder.' (I don't know the answer. — Would you know how to answer?)
exercises.explanation: 'Sé' = present of saber (I know). 'Sabrías' = conditional of saber (you would know). Saber uses the irregular stem sabr- in both future and conditional.
